content: The 2019 WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services include a detailed analysis of the cost-effectiveness of using dual HIV/syphilis tests during antenatal care (ANC) in settings with both high and low HIV prevalence. This analysis, led by Patricia Rodriguez and colleagues, utilized Markov decision-analytic models to evaluate the costs and infant health outcomes associated with maternal testing strategies. These strategies included testing at the first ANC visit using either individual tests (the base case) or a dual HIV/syphilis test. The study modeled scenarios in countries with high/intermediate HIV prevalence (South Africa and Kenya) and low HIV prevalence (Colombia and Ukraine). The findings demonstrated that routine testing at the first ANC visit with a dual HIV/syphilis test was cost-saving compared to individual tests. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) for dual testing were as follows: Kenya (-$23 per disability-adjusted life year [DALY] averted), South Africa (-$316 per DALY averted), Colombia (-$844 per DALY averted), and Ukraine (-$454 per DALY averted). Routine retesting with individual tests was cost-effective in Kenya (ICER: $437 per DALY averted) and Colombia (ICER: $2,685 per DALY averted) when compared to individual testing at the first ANC visit. The study concluded that incorporating dual HIV/syphilis testing into ANC services is either cost-effective or cost-saving across countries with varying HIV prevalence. This approach supports the dual elimination of mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV and congenital syphilis. Based on these findings, WHO recommends that all pregnant women be tested for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) at least once, ideally during their first ANC visit. This recommendation is particularly emphasized in settings where HBsAg seroprevalence is ≥2% in the general population. The dual HIV/syphilis test is a single, point-of-care rapid diagnostic test that simplifies the testing process. In contrast, individual tests involve separate rapid HIV tests and laboratory-based syphilis tests, such as the rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test and confirmatory Treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay (TPHA). Late ANC testing, defined as occurring between 36 and 39 weeks of gestation, was also considered in the modeling scenarios. The health impact and cost-effectiveness analysis revealed that dual testing at the first ANC visit reduced total costs and averted more DALYs compared to individual testing. For example, in Kenya, dual testing at the first ANC visit resulted in a cost reduction of $226,571 and averted 9,771 DALYs compared to the base case. Similar cost savings and health benefits were observed in South Africa, Colombia, and Ukraine. In summary, the study highlights the significant economic and health benefits of implementing dual HIV/syphilis testing in ANC services. This strategy not only improves maternal and child health outcomes but also aligns with global efforts to eliminate MTCT of HIV and congenital syphilis.
